title: How the power of voice, performance and authentic relationships has transformed the lives of secondary students excluded from mainstream school
author: Sharon Gray
summary: Gray, head of English and oracy at a Coventry alternative provision academy, argues that speech is the lever that reconnects permanently excluded teenagers to education. She opens with the student who arrives with dead eyes and head on the table, then describes the deliberate sequence she uses to change that: a classroom arranged as a hospitable room, a reset between lessons, and a portfolio of each student's genuine interests alongside the topics that must not be raised. Her claim is that oracy does therapeutic as well as academic work, letting students verbalise trauma and take it out of the body, and that relational talk has identifiable components rather than being a matter of warmth alone. The second half turns to concrete classroom strategies, including film trailer talk, painterly prompts with paint chart adjectives, food visuals, retuning voices against professional recordings, a formal newsdesk for code switching, and a Macbeth lesson built around prop blood and the save the last word for me routine. Gray grounds the approach in Mercer, Quigley and Page and Howe, and closes with a year eleven student's account of moving from being shown up in mainstream lessons to performing at the Belgrade Theatre.
points: Gray treats oracy as the entry point for students excluded from mainstream school, arguing that finding a true voice channels rage and unlocks latent talent.
She details the relational groundwork, including a reset classroom, recorded personal interests, and explicit notes on subjects that must be avoided with individual students.
She names the components of successful relationship talk and warns that any hint of being patronised reads as a red flag to these students.
The article supplies replicable strategies such as Film Trailer Talk, Painterly Prompts, Food Focus, Retuning Voices and the Code Switch Charm newsdesk, each with a student response attached.
A Macbeth sequence shows oracy feeding directly into GCSE written work, with prop blood and journalistic interviewing used to anchor quotations in memory.
quotes: Enabling students to find their true voice is the key to channelling their rage, unlocking their talent and creative potential. My job is to reanimate them, allow them to believe in themselves and to feel safe and included in school life - often for the first time in their lives.
Slowly we show them an alternative way school can be; a place where adults speak to students with respectful kindness, allowing each student to feel valued, have space to breathe and think deeply.

Oracy enables students to put their dreams and nightmare into words. It enables them to verbalise trauma, take it out of their body and up into the air, removing toxicity from their system. Words shape visions and concepts; articulate our past, present and future.

Listening to students is critical. We can’t pretend to hear or give students a cursory nod or glance. They have often been ignored at school and home. Not feeling heard or validated, they often just close up or react with anger.
The more golden coins of trust and respect you can put in the relationship bank, the more profitable the relationship.

The core elements of successful relationship talk are genuine interest, trust, respect, praise, humour, pace and appropriate tone. Any signs of being dismissed or being patronised are serious red flags for our students and they will often react negatively very quickly.
Oracy, woven into a creative curriculum of performance, music and media, has been transformative within our school, especially for year 10 and 11 students.
